abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces the Hierarchical Abstract Semantic Network (HASN), a novel knowledge representation paradigm that fundamentally rethinks how abstract concepts and their relationships are encoded in knowledge-based systems. Unlike traditional frame-based or ontological approaches that rely on static taxonomic structures, HASN employs a multi-layered abstraction mechanism where semantic relationships are dynamically established through cross-level inference channels. The core innovation lies in the introduction of conceptual anchoring operators that bind abstract predicates to concrete instances via contextual mediation functions, enabling formal reasoning across arbitrary abstraction depths while maintaining semantic coherence. We formally prove that HASN subsumes classical description logics in expressive power while overcoming their well-known limitation in handling higher-order knowledge and analogical reasoning. The computational complexity of reasoning procedures is shown to be polynomial-time decidable under reasonable structural constraints. Experimental validation through benchmark ontologies in the medical and engineering domains demonstrates that HASN-based representations achieve 34% improvement in inference coverage compared to state-of-the-art description logic systems while preserving computational tractability. This work establishes a new theoretical foundation for knowledge engineering that bridges symbolic reasoning and conceptual abstraction, with implications for expert systems, semantic web applications, and automated knowledge acquisition.

This paper presents a significant theoretical advancement in probabilistic logic programming by introducing the Granular Probability Logic Framework (GPLF), which substantially extends the expressiveness and reasoning capabilities of existing probabilistic knowledge bases. Traditional probabilistic logic systems, including Markov Logic Networks and ProbLog, suffer from limitations in handling multi-granular uncertainty where probabilities exist at different levels of abstraction. GPLF addresses this fundamental challenge by integrating granular computing principles with probabilistic semantics through a unified mathematical formalism. The framework introduces granular probability distributions that operate across multiple granularity levels, coupled with novel inference operators that enable cross-granular reasoning while preserving semantic consistency. We derive theoretical results establishing the conditions under which GPLF maintains logical entailment properties and propose an approximate inference algorithm with provable error bounds. Comparative evaluation on standard benchmarks in decision support and medical diagnosis demonstrates that GPLF achieves up to 28% improvement in prediction accuracy over contemporary probabilistic logic methods while exhibiting comparable computational efficiency. The framework provides a principled theoretical advancement that enables knowledge-based systems to represent and reason with uncertainty at multiple abstraction levels, representing a substantial improvement over prior approaches in the field of intelligent systems and reasoning under uncertainty.

This paper presents KAE-DSS, a knowledge-augmented expert system for decision support that introduces a fundamental paradigm shift in how domain expertise is integrated with machine learning predictions. Existing decision support systems typically treat symbolic knowledge and learned models as separate components, leading to opacity and integration challenges. KAE-DSS implements a novel Neural-Symbolic Integration Architecture (NSIA) where knowledge graphs and deep neural networks are deeply intertwined through learned embedding spaces that preserve symbolic semantics. The system features a knowledge-guided attention mechanism that allows neural predictions to be dynamically constrained and explained by expert-defined rules, and a rule extraction module that synthesizes neural network behavior into interpretable symbolic knowledge. We describe the complete system implementation including the knowledge acquisition pipeline, the neural-symbolic fusion engine, and the interactive explanation interface. Extensive evaluation on healthcare and financial decision tasks shows that KAE-DSS achieves 15% higher accuracy than pure ML approaches while providing actionable explanations grounded in domain knowledge. The system has been deployed in real-world settings, demonstrating practical viability and significant improvements in user trust and adoption rates.

This paper introduces an enhanced case-based reasoning system with adaptive retrieval and adaptation mechanisms designed to significantly improve upon conventional CBR approaches in dynamic problem-solving environments. Traditional CBR systems face well-known challenges including shallow case representation, limited semantic matching capabilities, and static adaptation rules that fail to capture domain complexity. The proposed system, AdaptiveCBR, incorporates three key architectural innovations: a multi-modal case representation framework integrating structural, temporal, and contextual features; a deep learning-powered retrieval engine combining semantic and structural similarity metrics through learned attention-weighted fusion; and a knowledge-driven adaptation module that applies expert-defined transformation rules augmented with learned pattern recognition. We present a comprehensive system architecture including the knowledge management subsystem, the retrieval optimization layer, and the user interaction framework. Empirical evaluation across customer service, technical support, and medical diagnosis domains reveals substantial improvements: retrieval precision increases by 32%, adaptation success rate improves by 41%, and overall problem resolution time decreases by 27% compared to state-of-the-art CBR systems. The system demonstrates significant practical value through successful deployment in production environments handling high-volume query streams.
